activity.hint: map returns a new array of the chosen property.

quiz.q: In K extends keyof T, what is K restricted to?
quiz.why: keyof T is the union of T's property names.

options: No, types are erased on compile
quiz.why: TypeScript types are removed; they give no runtime validation.

quiz.q: first<T>(arr: T[]) called with string[] returns?
quiz.why: T is inferred as string; empty arrays give undefined.

options: Using as to silence a type error
quiz.why: Casting hides real mismatches; fix the underlying type.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – validate untyped input at the boundary

scenes.text: An API handler receives JSON typed as any. A bad client sends age: "x".
Types cannot protect you here; the check must run at runtime, once, at the edge, producing a trusted type.
Libraries such as Zod or Valibot do this; you will write the core idea by hand.

steps.title: Parse, don't assume
steps.body: Take `unknown`, return a result union: `{ok:true,value}` or `{ok:false,error}`. After the boundary, internal code uses the precise type and never re-checks.

steps.title: Checklist
steps.body:
- Is it a non-null object?
- Does each field exist with the right typeof?
- Are business rules met (non-empty, range)?
- Report the first failing field name.

steps.title: Production practice
steps.body: Validate request bodies, query strings, environment variables and third-party responses. Return HTTP 400 or 422 with the field name, never a stack trace.

activity.prompt: Write parseUser(input) returning {ok:true,value:{name,age}} when name is a non-empty string and age is a number; else {ok:false,error:'name'} or 'age' (name checked first). The test loop prints results.

tests.expect:
ok Asha
error name
error age

activity.hint: Check name first, then age, then return the value.

quiz.q: Why validate at runtime if you use TypeScript?
options: Types are erased and cannot check external data
quiz.why: External data arrives at runtime; only runtime checks can verify it.

quiz.q: Best place to validate request data?
options: Once at the boundary where data enters
quiz.why: Parse once at the edge and pass trusted types inward.

quiz.q: Which status suits a body that fails validation?
quiz.why: It is a client error; 400 or 422 are the usual codes.

quiz.q: What should an error response avoid?
quiz.why: Stack traces expose internals and help attackers.

questions.q: Which narrows a value of type string | number to string?
questions.why: typeof guards narrow within the branch.
unknown is type-safe; any disables checks.
The shared literal tag drives narrowing.

options: A newly added variant with no handling case
questions.why: The leftover type is no longer never so compile fails.

questions.q: Area of circle r=1 rounded to 2 decimals?
Case: a handler does `const u = JSON.parse(body) as User` then reads u.age.toFixed(). A client sends age as a string. What happens?
options: Runtime TypeError, because as does not validate
questions.why: Assertions are erased; strings have no toFixed.

questions.q: Assertion: Generics are checked at runtime. Reason: They are retained in JavaScript output. Which is correct?
questions.why: Type parameters are erased during compilation.
K must be an actual key of T.

questions.q: Which state model prevents loading and error being set together?
questions.why: Each variant carries only its valid fields.

questions.q: Best response for failed body validation?
questions.why: Client errors get 4xx with a helpful, safe message.
map returns one item per element.

questions.q: A function parse(input: unknown) first does `if (typeof input !== 'object' || input === null) fail`. Why check null?
questions.why: Without the null check, property access on null would throw.

questions.q: Which is the most type-safe way to handle a third-party JSON response?
options: Validate with a runtime schema, then use the inferred type
questions.why: A runtime schema makes the static type truthful.

courses.title: REST API design in practice
courses.summary: Resource naming, HTTP methods and status codes, pagination, idempotency and consistent error bodies, practised through sorting, scenario and code labs. Goes beyond basic Node/Express routing.
outcomes: Design resource-oriented URLs
Pick correct methods and status codes
Compute and implement pagination

lessons.title: Lab: Sort URLs into good and bad designs

scenes.text: A mobile team inherits an API with /getUser, /deleteUserById and /doPayment.
New developers cannot guess any URL. The fix is nouns for resources and HTTP methods for actions.

steps.title: Resource-oriented design
steps.body: URLs name **things** (plural nouns): `/users`, `/users/42`, `/users/42/orders`. The **method** says what to do: GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partial update, DELETE remove.

steps.title: Conventions
steps.body:
- Lowercase, hyphenated paths
- Plural collections
- Nest only one or two levels
- Filters go in the query string: `/orders?status=paid`

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Verbs in paths (`/createOrder`) and GET requests that change data. GET must be safe: crawlers and prefetchers call it freely.

steps.title: Safe and idempotent
steps.body: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS are safe. GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent: repeating gives the same server state. POST is neither by default.

activity.prompt: Is each endpoint well designed?

quiz.why: Repeating the same PUT leaves the same state; POST may create duplicates.

options: In the body of a GET
Caches, crawlers and prefetch call it without user intent
quiz.why: Unsafe GETs can be triggered accidentally.

quiz.q: Best path for a user's orders?
quiz.why: Nested plural nouns express the relationship.

lessons.title: Lab: Choose the right status code

scenes.text: An API returns 200 with {"error":"not found"}. Monitoring shows 100% success while users see failures.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Families
steps.body: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

steps.title: Key codes
steps.body:
- 200 OK, 201 Created (with Location), 204 No Content
- 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthenticated, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable, 429 Too Many Requests
- 500 Internal Error, 503 Unavailable

steps.title: 401 vs 403
steps.body: 401 means we do not know who you are (missing or invalid credentials). 403 means we know you, but you are not allowed.

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the status code
pairs: Valid token but not your data
Too many requests in a minute

quiz.q: Successful POST that creates a resource?
quiz.why: 201 Created, ideally with a Location header.
429 Too Many Requests, often with Retry-After.

quiz.q: Logged-in user reads another user's invoice?
quiz.why: 403, or 404 if you prefer not to reveal existence.
A server-side fault; 503 signals temporary unavailability.

lessons.title: Lab: Pagination arithmetic

scenes.text: GET /orders returned every row and timed out. Pagination fixes it.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Offset vs cursor
steps.body:
**Offset**: `?page=3&size=20` becomes `LIMIT 20 OFFSET (page-1)*size`. Simple, but deep pages are slow and rows shift when data changes.

**Cursor (keyset)**: `?after=<last id>` becomes `WHERE id > :after ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`. Stable and fast with an index.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Page 3, size 20 gives offset (3-1)×20 = 40. Total pages for 95 rows = ceil(95/20) = 5.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Allowing unbounded `size`. Always cap it (e.g. 100) on the server.

activity.prompt: What SQL OFFSET is needed for page 7 with page size 25?

quiz.q: Total pages for 95 rows at size 20?
Why prefer cursor pagination for large feeds?
options: Stable results and index-friendly speed on deep pages
quiz.why: Keyset avoids scanning skipped rows and tolerates inserts.
Unbounded sizes are a denial-of-service risk.

lessons.title: Lab: Safe retries with idempotency keys

scenes.text: A customer taps Pay on a flaky network. The app times out and retries.
The server had processed the first request. Without protection, the card is charged twice.

steps.title: Idempotency-Key
steps.body: The client sends a unique key (such as a UUID) in an `Idempotency-Key` header with the POST. The server stores the key and the result. A repeat with the same key returns the stored result and does nothing new.

steps.title: Implementation notes
steps.body:
- Store key with a request fingerprint
- Same key, different body: reject with 422 or 409
- Expire keys after a window (e.g. 24 hours)
- Make storing the key and creating the charge atomic

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

a.text: The mobile app times out on POST /payments and the user taps Pay again. How should the client retry?

choices.label: Resend with a NEW random key
choices.feedback: A new key looks like a new payment.

choices.label: Resend with the SAME Idempotency-Key
choices.feedback: Correct: the server can detect the duplicate.

bad.text: The customer is charged twice. Support ticket raised.

ok.text: The server returns the stored result of the first charge. One payment only.

quiz.q: Same key, different request body: best response?
quiz.why: The key is being reused incorrectly.
Repeating them yields the same state.
The client must reuse it across retries.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – consistent error responses

scenes.text: One endpoint returns {err}, another {message}, another HTML. Client code is full of special cases.
RFC 9457 Problem Details defines one JSON shape with type, title, status, detail and instance.

steps.title: Problem Details
steps.body: Content type `application/problem+json`. Fields: `type` (URI identifying the problem), `title` (short, stable), `status`, `detail` (specific to this occurrence), `instance`. Extensions such as `errors` for field problems are allowed.

steps.title: Do not leak
steps.body: Never include stack traces, SQL or internal hostnames in detail.

courses.title: Perceptrons and multilayer networks by hand

lessons.title: Lab: Train a perceptron by hand

scenes.text: An AND gate: output 1 only when both inputs are 1.
Update weights only on mistakes.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: ŷ = 1 if w·x + b > 0 else 0. For each example: w ← w + η(y − ŷ)x, b ← b + η(y − ŷ). Converges if the data are linearly separable (perceptron convergence theorem).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: η=1, w=(0,0), b=0. Example (1,1), y=1: ŷ=0 → w=(1,1), b=1. Example (0,0), y=0: z=1 → ŷ=1 → error −1 → w stays (1,1), b=0. Continue until all four are correct.

steps.title: Check your work
steps.body:
- Print intermediate values and compare with a hand calculation on a tiny example.
- Keep a fixed seed or fixed data while debugging.
- Re-run from a clean start before trusting the result.

lessons.title: Lab: XOR needs a hidden layer

scenes.text: XOR: 1 when inputs differ.
No single line separates the classes.

steps.title: Why
steps.body: XOR points (0,0),(1,1)→0 and (0,1),(1,0)→1: any line putting both 1s above leaves a 0 on the wrong side. A hidden layer composes OR and NAND: XOR = AND(OR(a,b), NAND(a,b)).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Hidden h1 = step(a+b−0.5) (OR), h2 = step(1.5−a−b) (NAND), output = step(h1+h2−1.5) (AND). For (1,0): h1=1,h2=1 → out step(0.5)=1 ✓. For (1,1): h2=0 → out 0 ✓.

steps.body: A diamond |x|+|y| < 1 can be built with ReLU units: |x| = ReLU(x)+ReLU(−x). So |x|+|y| = sum of four ReLUs; output = step(1 − sum).

courses.title: Backpropagation by hand and from scratch
courses.summary: Derive and compute backpropagation for a tiny network, implement a two-layer net on XOR in pure Python, and verify with gradient checking.

lessons.title: Lab: Backprop through one neuron by hand

scenes.text: A single sigmoid neuron with squared loss.
Chain rule flows from loss back to weights.

steps.title: Chain
steps.body: z = wx + b; a = σ(z); L = ½(a − y)². dL/da = a−y; da/dz = a(1−a); dz/dw = x. So dL/dw = (a−y)·a(1−a)·x.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Dropping the a(1−a) factor — the 'saturating' term that causes vanishing gradients.

activity.prompt: Compute dL/dw for x=1, w=0.5, b=0, y=1 with sigmoid and L=½(a−y)² (4 decimals).

lessons.title: Lab: Two-layer network on XOR from scratch

scenes.text: Train 2→3→1 sigmoid network on XOR.
Forward, backward, update.

steps.title: Deltas
steps.body: Output delta δ₂ = (a₂−y)·a₂(1−a₂). Hidden delta δ₁ = (W₂ᵀδ₂) ⊙ a₁(1−a₁). Gradients: dW₂ = δ₂a₁ᵀ, dW₁ = δ₁xᵀ; biases get the deltas.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: If δ₂=−0.1 and the connection weights from three hidden units are (0.4,−0.2,0.7), hidden error signals before the sigmoid factor are (−0.04, 0.02, −0.07).

steps.title: Initialise small random weights
steps.body: All-zero weights keep hidden units identical (symmetry).

activity.prompt: Train a 2-3-1 sigmoid network on XOR (seed 1, η=1, 5000 epochs) and print the rounded outputs.
activity.starter:
import random
from math import exp
rng = random.Random(1)
sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
W1 = [[rng.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in range(2)] for _ in range(3)]
b1 = [0.0] * 3
W2 = [rng.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in range(3)]
b2 = 0.0
X = [(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)]
Y = [0, 1, 1, 0]
for _ in range(5000):
    for x, y in zip(X, Y):
        a1 = [sig(sum(W1[j][i] * x[i] for i in range(2)) + b1[j]) for j in range(3)]
        a2 = sig(sum(W2[j] * a1[j] for j in range(3)) + b2)
        d2 = (a2 - y) * a2 * (1 - a2)
        # TODO: hidden deltas
        for j in range(3):
            W2[j] -= d2 * a1[j]
            b1[j] -= d1[j]
            for i in range(2):
                W1[j][i] -= d1[j] * x[i]
        b2 -= d2
out = []
for x in X:
    a1 = [sig(sum(W1[j][i] * x[i] for i in range(2)) + b1[j]) for j in range(3)]
    out.append(round(sig(sum(W2[j] * a1[j] for j in range(3)) + b2)))
print(out)
activity.solution:
import random
from math import exp
rng = random.Random(1)
sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
W1 = [[rng.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in range(2)] for _ in range(3)]
b1 = [0.0] * 3
W2 = [rng.uniform(-1, 1) for _ in range(3)]
b2 = 0.0
X = [(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)]
Y = [0, 1, 1, 0]
for _ in range(5000):
    for x, y in zip(X, Y):
        a1 = [sig(sum(W1[j][i] * x[i] for i in range(2)) + b1[j]) for j in range(3)]
        a2 = sig(sum(W2[j] * a1[j] for j in range(3)) + b2)
        d2 = (a2 - y) * a2 * (1 - a2)
        d1 = [d2 * W2[j] * a1[j] * (1 - a1[j]) for j in range(3)]
        for j in range(3):
            W2[j] -= d2 * a1[j]
            b1[j] -= d1[j]
            for i in range(2):
                W1[j][i] -= d1[j] * x[i]
        b2 -= d2
out = []

lessons.title: Lab: SGD, momentum and Adam updates

scenes.text: A ravine-shaped loss: steep in one direction, shallow in another.
Momentum and adaptive rates help.

steps.title: Updates
steps.body: SGD: w ← w − ηg. Momentum: v ← βv + g; w ← w − ηv. Adam: m ← β₁m+(1−β₁)g; v ← β₂v+(1−β₂)g²; m̂=m/(1−β₁ᵗ); v̂=v/(1−β₂ᵗ); w ← w − η m̂/(√v̂+ε). Defaults β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, ε=1e-8.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: First Adam step with g=2, η=0.1: m=0.2, v=0.004; m̂=2, v̂=4 → step = 0.1·2/2 = **0.1** — about η regardless of the gradient scale.

steps.title: Why bias correction
steps.body: m and v start at 0, so early estimates are biased low.

    m = b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g
    v = b2 * v + (1 - b2) * g * g
    # TODO: bias-corrected moments
    w -= lr * mh / (sqrt(vh) + eps)
    print(round(w, 5))

from math import sqrt
w, m, v = 1.0, 0.0, 0.0
b1, b2, lr, eps, g = 0.9, 0.999, 0.1, 1e-8, 2.0

    m = b1 * m + (1 - b1) * g
    v = b2 * v + (1 - b2) * g * g

steps.title: Recurrence
steps.body: r₀=1, j₀=1. For each layer: r ← r + (k−1)·j; j ← j·s. (r = receptive field, j = jump between neighbouring outputs.)

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Three 3×3 conv layers (stride 1): r = 1+2=3, 5, **7**. Two 3×3 convs equal one 5×5 receptive field with fewer parameters (2·9 vs 25 per channel pair).

steps.title: Mechanisms

lessons.title: Lab: Standardise, normalise and log-transform

scenes.text: Income is in lakhs, age in years — distance-based models get dominated by income.
Scaling puts features on comparable footing.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: **Standardise**: z=(x−μ)/σ (mean 0, sd 1). **Min-max**: (x−min)/(max−min) ∈[0,1]. **Log**: log(1+x) tames right skew. Tree models don't need scaling; kNN, SVM, k-means, neural nets and regularised linear models do.

steps.title: Leakage
steps.body: Compute μ, σ, min, max from **training** data and apply to test data — never refit on test.

steps.title: Encoders
steps.body: **One-hot**: one 0/1 column per category (drop one to avoid collinearity). **Ordinal**: only if a true order exists (S<M<L). **Target encoding**: replace category by the mean target — powerful but leaky; use out-of-fold means with smoothing: (n·mean_cat + m·mean_global)/(n+m).

class Pipe:
    def fit(self, rows):
        v = [r[0] for r in rows]
        self.mu = sum(v) / len(v)
        self.sd = (sum((x - self.mu) ** 2 for x in v) / len(v)) ** 0.5
        self.cats = sorted({r[1] for r in rows})
        return self
    def transform(self, rows):
        return [[round((n - self.mu) / self.sd, 2)] + [int(c == k) for k in self.cats] for n, c in rows]

lessons.title: Lab: Mutual information

story.title: Which column tells us about churn?

scenes.text: Does 'plan' or 'city' say more about churn?
Mutual information measures dependence in bits.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: I(X;Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X) = Σ p(x,y) log₂ [p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y))]. It is 0 iff X and Y are independent and works for non-linear dependence.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: If X perfectly determines a fair binary Y, I = H(Y) = **1 bit**. If independent, I = 0.

steps.title: Check your work

for a in (0, 1):

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: TP, FP, FN, TN. Accuracy=(TP+TN)/n; Precision=TP/(TP+FP); Recall (sensitivity)=TP/(TP+FN); Specificity=TN/(TN+FP); F1 = 2PR/(P+R) (harmonic mean).

steps.title: Mistake

lessons.title: Lab: Accuracy paradox and MCC

scenes.text: A fraud model flags nothing.
MCC reveals the truth that accuracy hides.

steps.title: MCC
steps.body: MCC = (TP·TN − FP·FN)/√((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)), range −1..1; 0 = no better than chance. Balanced accuracy = (recall + specificity)/2.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 1000 transactions, 10 fraud. Model predicts all normal: TP=0, FN=10, FP=0, TN=990. Accuracy 99%; recall 0; balanced accuracy = (0+1)/2 = **0.5**; MCC = 0 (denominator 0 → defined as 0).

steps.title: Use several metrics
steps.body: No single number fits every problem.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: TPR = TP/(TP+FN) (recall); FPR = FP/(FP+TN). Sweep thresholds from high to low; the curve goes from (0,0) to (1,1). Random classifier = diagonal; perfect = (0,1) corner.

steps.title: z-test
steps.body: p̂₁ = x₁/n₁, p̂₂ = x₂/n₂, pooled p̂ = (x₁+x₂)/(n₁+n₂). SE = √(p̂(1−p̂)(1/n₁+1/n₂)). z = (p̂₂ − p̂₁)/SE. |z| > 1.96 ⇒ p < 0.05 (two-sided).

steps.title: Peeking
steps.body: Checking the result daily and stopping when p<0.05 inflates false positives; fix the sample size in advance.

# TODO: test statistic

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: For vectors a, b ∈ ℝⁿ: **a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ**. The **L2 norm** is ‖a‖ = √(a·a). The **L1 norm** is Σ|aᵢ|. Unit vector = a/‖a‖.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Forgetting the square root in the norm.

lessons.title: Lab: Angle and cosine similarity

scenes.text: A search engine ranks documents by the angle between word-count vectors.
Small angle = similar content.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: cos θ = (a·b)/(‖a‖‖b‖). Value 1 means same direction, 0 orthogonal, −1 opposite. In text mining it is **cosine similarity**.

steps.title: Scale invariance
steps.body: Cosine ignores vector length: a document repeated twice has the same cosine with a query.

activity.prompt: Compute cosine similarity of (1, 2, 3) and (2, 4, 6), and of (1, 0) and (0, 5); print 4 decimals.
activity.starter:
from math import sqrt
def cos(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    na = sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    nb = sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    # TODO: dot over product of norms
print(round(cos([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6]), 4), round(cos([1, 0], [0, 5]), 4))
activity.solution:
from math import sqrt
def cos(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    na = sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    nb = sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    return dot / (na * nb)
print(round(cos([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6]), 4), round(cos([1, 0], [0, 5]), 4))

lessons.title: Lab: Projection and independence

scenes.text: The shadow of a stick on the ground is a projection.

steps.title: Projection
steps.body: Projection of a onto b: **proj_b(a) = (a·b / b·b) b**. Scalar part = a·b/‖b‖. Vectors are **linearly independent** if no one is a combination of the others; in 2-D, (a₁,a₂),(b₁,b₂) are independent iff a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ ≠ 0.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: a=(3,4), b=(1,0): a·b=3, b·b=1 → projection = (3,0). Residual (0,4) is orthogonal to b: (0,4)·(1,0)=0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by ‖b‖ instead of b·b for the vector form.
- Assuming perpendicular means independent only; any non-parallel pair is independent.

lessons.title: Lab: Matrix multiplication and shapes

story.title: One layer of a neural net

scenes.text: A layer maps 3 inputs to 2 outputs with a 2×3 weight matrix.
Shapes must match: (m×n)(n×p) = (m×p).

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: (AB)ᵢⱼ = Σₖ Aᵢₖ Bₖⱼ. Inner dimensions must agree; the result has the outer dimensions. Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**: AB ≠ BA generally; it is associative.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying element-wise (that is the Hadamard product).
- Ignoring shapes: (2×3)(2×3) is undefined.

activity.prompt: Write matmul(A, B) with nested loops and print A·B for A=[[1,2],[3,4]], B=[[5,6],[7,8]].
activity.starter:
def matmul(A, B):
    n, m, p = len(A), len(B), len(B[0])
    # TODO: row-by-column sums
print(matmul([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[5, 6], [7, 8]]))
activity.solution:
def matmul(A, B):
    n, m, p = len(A), len(B), len(B[0])
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(m)) for j in range(p)] for i in range(n)]
print(matmul([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[5, 6], [7, 8]]))

steps.title: 2×2 formulas

steps.title: Pitfall
steps.body: log 0 is undefined; clip probabilities (e.g. 1e-12).

scenes.text: With few rows and many features, weights explode.

steps.title: Ridge
steps.body: Loss = MSE + λΣwⱼ² (don't penalise the intercept). Gradient adds 2λwⱼ. Closed form: (XᵀX + λI)β = Xᵀy — also fixes singular XᵀX. Larger λ → smaller weights, more bias, less variance.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Data y=2x exactly (x=1,2,3). OLS w=2. Ridge λ=1 on centred data shrinks: w = Sxy/(Sxx+λ) = 4/(2+1) = **1.333**.

steps.title: Standardise
steps.body: Always standardise features before ridge/lasso — the penalty is scale-sensitive.

def s(p, own, other):
    a = sum(abs(p - q) for q in own if q != p) / (len(own) - 1)
    b = sum(abs(p - q) for q in other) / len(other)

steps.title: k-means++
steps.body: Pick the first centre at random; each next centre with probability proportional to D(x)², the squared distance to the nearest chosen centre. It spreads centres and gives a provable O(log k) approximation. Run several restarts and keep the lowest inertia.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Points 0, 1, 10 with the first centre at 0: D² = (0,1,100) → probability of choosing 10 is 100/101 = **0.990**.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: k-means assumes roughly spherical, similar-size clusters; use DBSCAN or Gaussian mixtures otherwise.
